title: Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation
summary: Alarm-and-warning evaluation is a diagnostic practice for examining the operational behaviour of alerts, warnings, and alarm states. It assesses priority hierarchy, actionability, communication channels, nuisance alarm exposure, mute behaviour, operating-condition performance, and relevant standards alignment.
keyFacts: The practice evaluates alerts, warnings, and alarm states against operating conditions rather than controlled viewing conditions.
The evaluation distinguishes technical presence from operational success: an alarm may be visible and accurately triggered but still fail if it does not communicate what to do.
Assessment topics include priority hierarchy, actionability, communication channels, nuisance alarm exposure, mute behaviour, operating-condition testing, and regulatory alignment.
In regulated medical device contexts, the evaluation includes assessment against IEC 60601-1-8 and is conducted through the IEC 62366-1 usability-engineering process.
IEC 62366-1 governs the usability-engineering process; it does not specify what an alarm must look or sound like.
The practice is used during Sandbox Experiments, complex product audits, and Iterative System Building in regulated medical device contexts.
The practice typically follows state-and-transition review and directly informs warning-and-alarm clarity improvement.

Documented engagement evidence includes deSoutter Medical / Zethon, Kardion MCS Controller, Cox Marine cluster displays, Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX, Gexcon CFD simulation, Streetec kntrl 2, the MDU ship motion monitoring system, Oceaneering, Raymarine, and Schone Airspace Group.
The Kardion case records that the design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required.
Several engagement examples explicitly describe designed responses rather than measured safety, efficiency, alarm-response, throughput, fleet, or commercial outcomes.

bodySections.heading: Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies alarm-and-warning evaluation as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: Definition and Scope of Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation is the assessment of alerts, warnings, and alarm states against the criteria that determine whether they will communicate correctly and remain actionable under real operating conditions.

The practice evaluates operational communication, not only technical display behaviour. An alarm can be technically present, visible, and accurately triggered while still failing operationally if it does not communicate the required action, cannot be distinguished from lower-priority alerts, or depends on a communication channel that degrades in the environment where the device is used.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation is an assessment activity applied to a specific system or proposed alarm architecture. It is not the full alarm-management discipline of lifecycle, rationalisation, priority assignment, and standards codification.

bodySections.heading: What Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation Assesses
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation asks whether an alarm can be perceived, interpreted, prioritised, and acted on in the environment where the device or system operates.

The core questions are whether the alarm can be perceived under actual lighting, noise, workload, and physical-position constraints; whether it can be interpreted quickly enough to act; whether it directs attention to the right place; and whether it communicates both the problem and the next step.

The practice treats operating conditions as part of the evaluation object. Controlled viewing conditions are insufficient when the real system is used under variable lighting, noise, vibration, divided attention, gloved interaction, or multi-device monitoring.

bodySections.heading: Priority Hierarchy and Actionability Assessment
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Priority hierarchy assessment checks whether the alarm system has a defined priority structure and whether that structure is expressed clearly enough for use.

The evaluation asks whether a user looking at an active alarm state can immediately tell whether the condition requires immediate intervention or is informational. When multiple alarms are active simultaneously, the highest-priority condition should receive the most prominent treatment.

Actionability assessment asks whether each warning or alarm communicates what to do, not only that something is wrong. In time-pressured environments, an alarm that communicates a condition without specifying the next action does not close the action loop.

bodySections.heading: Communication Channels and Operating-Condition Testing
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Communication channel analysis identifies which channels each alarm uses, including colour, sound, icon, position, text, and vibration. The evaluation checks whether an alarm depends on a single channel that may fail under operating conditions.

Colour-only indicators are unreliable in variable lighting. Sound-only alarms are vulnerable to noise. Text can become unreadable under vibration. Alarm-and-warning evaluation identifies these single-channel dependencies and records where redundant non-colour or non-auditory cues are needed.

Operating-condition testing evaluates significant alarms under the conditions of actual use. In embedded systems, alarm-and-warning evaluation must be conducted in the real environment or approximated to the real environment. The purpose is to assess whether the alarm works in use, not whether it is legible in isolation.

bodySections.heading: Nuisance Alarm Exposure and Mute Behaviour
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation examines how frequently alarms trigger under conditions that do not require action. Nuisance alarms are treated as a driver of alert fatigue because habitual dismissal of low-value alerts can extend to genuine alerts.

The evaluation estimates false positive exposure and identifies alarm types most likely to train dismissal behaviour. This is a diagnostic assessment of alarm architecture, not a claim that a particular system has produced a measured alarm-response outcome.

Mute behaviour review examines what happens when a user silences an alarm. The evaluation distinguishes muting that produces genuine silence from muting that makes an active alarm invisible. A muted alarm may need to remain visually present at reduced prominence; if an alarm disappears entirely when muted, the system creates a pathway to an active alarm state with no visible indication.

bodySections.heading: Regulatory and Standards Framing for Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In regulated medical device contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation includes assessment against IEC 60601-1-8, the collateral standard for alarm systems in medical electrical equipment.

The evaluation covers priority tiering requirements, the prohibition on colour as the sole differentiating attribute between priority levels, mute behaviour requirements, and alarm state visibility requirements.

IEC 62366-1 governs the usability-engineering process through which use-related risks behind alarm requirements are identified and evaluated. IEC 62366-1 does not specify what an alarm must look or sound like.

Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only. Summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

In applicable regulated contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation may also be framed by IEC 62682 and ISA-18.2 alarm-management standards. This page does not claim that any named non-medical engagement was certified to, audited against, or designed under those standards.

bodySections.heading: Where Creative Navy Uses Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy uses alarm-and-warning evaluation during Sandbox Experiments when reviewing an existing system. In that position, the practice contributes to the diagnostic evidence base established before design work begins.

Creative Navy also uses alarm-and-warning evaluation in complex product audits. Alarm architecture failures are a recurring finding in audits of high-consequence systems, and the evaluation provides structured evidence for specific recommendations.

In regulated medical device contexts, Creative Navy uses alarm-and-warning evaluation throughout Iterative System Building as part of the IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation process. Proposed alarm designs are assessed against IEC 60601-1-8 alarm-system requirements before they are finalised.

The practice typically follows state-and-transition review, which identifies system states including alarm states. It precedes the redesign work covered under warning-and-alarm clarity improvement and often runs in parallel with error-likely interaction review.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation produces diagnostic findings and design requirements.

The findings may identify single-channel alarm dependency, priority hierarchy ambiguity, actionability gaps, muting behaviour that hides active alarms, alert fatigue risk, or alarm states that are technically visible but operationally hard to locate.

The outputs can include specific alarm architecture requirements, such as redundant non-colour cues for critical states, two-level alarm architectures, separation of routine and critical notifications, multi-stage warning architecture, acknowledgement behaviour distinct from clearing, and owner-scoped alerts.

In regulated medical-device contexts, the output can be documented design requirements traceable to identified use-related hazards and evaluated during IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation against IEC 60601-1-8 alarm-system requirements.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries and Limits of Alarm-and-Warning Evaluation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Alarm-and-warning evaluation does not by itself constitute alarm lifecycle rationalisation. It evaluates the alarm and warning scheme of a system; the broader discipline of alarm lifecycle, rationalisation, and priority assignment belongs to alarm management.

The engagement evidence for alarm-and-warning evaluation must not be read as evidence of measured efficiency, error-rate, alarm-response, throughput, fleet, safety, commercial, rescue, distress-response, collision, flight-safety, airworthiness, or certification outcomes. Several examples describe designed responses, not deployed results.

Named non-medical examples that refer to standards are not conformance claims. ISA-18.2, IEC 62682, and IMO Bridge Alert Management frame relevant categories in the documented cases, but this page does not claim certification, audit, rationalisation, or compliance for those engagements.

The industrial automation audit findings are specific to one running system used in a machining-cell context. They must not be used as a general claim about industrial software and must not be used to support Oceaneering context material.

strongClaims: Alarm-and-warning evaluation assesses alerts, warnings, and alarm states against operating conditions rather than only checking whether they appear on screen.
The practice examines priority hierarchy, actionability, communication channels, nuisance alarm exposure, mute behaviour, operating-condition testing, and regulatory alignment.
In regulated medical device contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation includes assessment against IEC 60601-1-8 and is conducted through the IEC 62366-1 usability-engineering process.

The Kardion MCS Controller evaluation produced alarm architecture requirements traceable to identified use-related hazards, and the design passed FDA evaluation as submitted with no design changes required.
weakerClaims: The deSoutter Medical / Zethon evaluation assessed 6 comparable surgical devices under operating theatre conditions and identified colour-only communication as the primary failure mode across the competitive set.
The Cox Marine cluster displays evaluation identified that visible tile-level faults could still fail operationally when they did not direct attention to the priority engine.
The Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX evaluation identified alert fatigue risk from routine sensor-range notifications receiving the same treatment as critical failure alerts.
The MDU alarm scheme binds alarm state to rolling maximum and minimum values over the last twenty minutes rather than to the live instantaneous value.
The Oceaneering dispatch-panel state model separated sending and receiving states, reserved red for errors, and added non-colour channels, but this is not measured evidence of improved performance.

The Raymarine priority-and-arbitration scheme assigned event priority by consequence rather than arrival order and included duplicate coalescing, focus arbitration, permitted presentation surfaces, and conditional task restoration.
The Schone Airspace Group Mission Control design separated acknowledgement from clearing and kept alert ownership visible across compact alerts, fleet cards, inspectors, live notices, and history.
limitations: The page describes an evaluation practice, not the full alarm-management discipline of lifecycle, rationalisation, priority assignment, and standards codification.

Most engagement examples describe evaluation findings or designed responses; they are not evidence of measured safety, efficiency, alarm-response, throughput, fleet, commercial, rescue, distress-response, collision, airworthiness, or certification outcomes.

Non-medical references to ISA-18.2, IEC 62682, IMO Bridge Alert Management, IEC 62923-1, and IEC 62923-2 are framing references, not conformance, certification, audit, or rationalisation claims for the named engagements.
The industrial automation audit findings apply only to the specific machining-cell process control system reviewed and must not be generalised to industrial software.
The Oceaneering evidence reflects reported speech and expert judgement from operations stakeholders, not field observation or measured validation of design performance.
The Raymarine radio was built and released, but no fidelity comparison to the described scheme is recorded.
The Schone Airspace Group product was built and is in test, not deployed.
Streetec kntrl 2 regulatory constraints shaped the design, but no safety result was measured.
